svg.title: A toolbox release reaches a project that installed only source publication — the release updates the component and its spine, spares the team's rules, and brings nothing else
svg.text: A toolbox release reaches a project that installed only
Scenario: the release updates the component and its spine, spares the team's rules, and brings nothing else

g.text: Given a project that installed source publication and nothing else
A project that ticked source publication on the installer's checklist and nothing else. Its
own README and src are there; the install added three things beside them, .config, .env.dist
and Taskfile.yml, and five entries under .config. Sixteen files in all, and the last line is
the release they came from.
What is NOT there is the point: no linter, no container runtime, no forge tooling, and not
even the phase orchestrators a full project gets. Only what runs the publication and what
keeps it up to date.
And what it would publish today, cluster credential included
What the project would publish today. Three files, and among them src/cluster.kubeconfig, a
cluster credential that nobody thought to deny.
Remember this list. The same command answers differently four cards from here, without
anyone touching a single rule.
When a new toolbox release arrives and the update runs
A new toolbox release lands. This is the exact command Renovate runs in a real repository
when it opens the framework-evolution merge request; nothing here is a stand-in for it.
Then the project tracks the new release, and git says exactly what
moved
The version line moved to the new release, and under it git says exactly what came with it:
the machinery that performed the update, and the publication floor the framework owns.
Three files. That is the whole update for this project, and it is the shape the story is
here to guarantee.
And the rules the team wrote came through untouched
The two files that carry the team's own decisions, before and after: git reports no change
at all on them, and their contents are what the team wrote.
That is copier's three-way merge doing the work. A release edits the files the framework
owns and leaves the ones the project owns alone, which for a manifest that decides what
becomes public is the whole point.
And the tightened floor from that release is already in force
The same command as four cards ago, and a different answer: src/cluster.kubeconfig is now
held back, by the framework floor, because the new release added that rule to it.
Nobody edited a list. The project got a tightened safety floor from the release itself,
which is exactly why a component that cannot be updated is worse than no component.
And nothing the project never installed arrived with it
The same two listings as the opening card, unchanged. The release also changed a tool this
project never installed, and that change did not arrive.
An update applies to what you have. It does not quietly grow your project back into the
whole framework, which is what makes taking one component a real choice rather than a first
step.
